section: Form as a function of growth rates
label: External form results from the ratio of growth rates in different directions
claim: Except for certain very minute organisms whose form is set directly by molecular forces, the external form of an organism is accounted for by the ratio between its rates of growth in different directions.
quote: It is the ratio between the rates of growth in various directions by which we must account for the external forms of all, save certain very minute, organisms.
scope: all organisms except very minute ones (e.g. single small cells shaped by surface tension)
measurable_quantities: directional growth rates (length, breadth, depth per unit time)
candidate_data: Longitudinal morphometric growth series and 3D developmental image time-lapses (e.g. published ontogenetic shape datasets on Dryad, MorphoSource specimen series).

section: Form as a function of growth rates
label: Constant growth-rate ratios preserve form; changing ratios produce development
claim: When the ratio between growth rates in different directions stays constant, an organism grows in bulk with little or no change of form; such constancy seldom lasts more than a season, and when the ratio alters the organism undergoes development, a steady and persistent change of form.
quote: It may sometimes be a very _constant_ one, in which case the organism, while growing in bulk, suffers little or no perceptible change in form; but such equilibrium seldom endures for more than a season, and when the _ratio_ tends to alter, then we have the phenomenon of morphological “development,” or steady and persistent change of form.
measurable_quantities: ratios of linear dimensions over age
rate of change of shape indices
candidate_data: Longitudinal growth and shape datasets for animals and plants (e.g. ontogenetic morphometric series on Dryad, human growth cohort data).

label: Embryonic folds arise from local differences in growth rate of a uniform sheet
claim: The foldings of the blastoderm that produce the neural and amniotic folds result from unequal rates of growth, local accelerations and retardations, in what is at first an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue, in the way that a sheet buckles when parts of it expand or contract.
quote: the various foldings of the blastoderm, by which the neural and amniotic folds were brought into being, were essentially and obviously the resultant of unequal rates of growth,—of local accelerations or retardations of growth,—in what to begin with was an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue.
scope: vertebrate embryos (blastoderm / germinal disc), especially the chick
measurable_quantities: local tissue growth rates (cell proliferation, area expansion)
candidate_data: Live-imaging and cell-tracking datasets of chick and other vertebrate embryos during neurulation (e.g. Image Data Resource entries, published tissue-growth maps).

label: Differences between related forms emerge gradually and are small in the young
claim: Because form differences are attained by growth at specific velocities over long periods, differences between any two related individuals or species must appear gradually and be little apparent in the young, and animals of very different adult size differ less and less in size and form when traced back through foetal stages.
quote: it is accordingly obvious that in any two related individuals (whether specifically identical or not) the differences between them must manifest themselves gradually, and be but little apparent in the young. It is for the same simple reason that animals which are of very different sizes when adult, differ less and less in size (as well as in form) as we trace them backwards through the foetal stages.
scope: related individuals and species, especially mammals with foetal development
measurable_quantities: size and shape divergence between species across developmental stages
foetal body size by gestational age across species
candidate_data: Comparative embryo and foetal growth series and ontogenetic morphometric datasets (e.g. MorphoSource embryo scans, published comparative prenatal growth data).

label: Human stature grows fast in infancy, steadily in childhood, then quickens in the teens
claim: The human curve of growth in stature shows rapid increase in infancy, a long period of slower, nearly steady growth in early boyhood, a marked quickening in the early teens, and finally a gradual arrest as full height is reached.
quote: The curve of growth for length or stature in man indicates a rapid increase at the outset, that is to say during the quick growth of babyhood; a long period of slower, but still rapid and almost steady growth in early boyhood; as a rule a marked quickening soon after the boy is in his teens, when he comes to “the growing age”
candidate_data: WHO and CDC growth reference data and national longitudinal growth cohort datasets.

label: Adult human stature declines well before fifty and markedly by old age
claim: Full adult stature in man lasts only for a time: it begins to decrease well before fifty, is notably lessened by sixty, and is much reduced in extreme old age, so that growth takes a negative value.
quote: We should see that a man’s full stature endures but for a spell; long before fifty it has begun to abate, by sixty it is notably lessened, in extreme old age the old man’s frame is shrunken and it is but a memory that “he once was tall.”
candidate_data: Longitudinal ageing cohorts with repeated height measurement (e.g. Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, NHANES cross-sectional data).

label: Weight tends to vary as the cube of linear dimensions during growth
claim: Whatever the law of increase in a linear dimension, volume and therefore weight tend to vary as the cube of linear dimensions, which mainly (though not wholly) explains why the human weight curve differs in shape from the stature curve.
quote: whatever be the law of increment in a linear dimension, the law of increase in volume, and therefore in weight, will be that these latter magnitudes tend to vary as the cubes of the linear dimensions.
candidate_data: WHO/CDC growth references and longitudinal cohort data giving paired height and weight by age.

label: Boys and girls share a growth-velocity curve differing mainly in phase
claim: The curves of growth velocity in boys and girls are of very similar shape but differ in amplitude and especially in phase, the girl's adolescent acceleration beginning and ending earlier than the boy's.
quote: In short, throughout all this period, it is a very _similar_ curve in the two sexes; but it has its notable differences, in amplitude and especially in _phase_.
measurable_quantities: annual weight and height increments by age and sex
candidate_data: Sex-specific growth velocity references (WHO, CDC) and longitudinal cohort datasets.

label: All animals pass through the same phases of growth: slow start, early peak, slowdown
claim: In long-lived and short-lived animals alike, growth begins slowly, reaches its maximum velocity early, and then slows down (with temporary accelerations) toward a point where it ceases.
quote: Whether the animal be long-lived, as man or the elephant, or short-lived, like horse or dog, it passes through the same phases of growth. In all cases growth begins slowly; it attains a maximum velocity early in its course, and afterwards slows down (subject to temporary accelerations) towards a point where growth ceases altogether.
candidate_data: Comparative growth-curve compilations (e.g. AnAge, published vertebrate growth-curve datasets on Dryad).

label: Cold-blooded animals approach a maximal size only asymptotically
claim: In cold-blooded animals such as fishes the slowing of growth is greatly protracted, so that size seems never to reach a maximum but only to approach a limit asymptotically.
quote: But especially in the cold-blooded animals, such as fishes, the slowing-down period is very greatly protracted, and the size of the creature would seem never actually to reach, but only to approach asymptotically, to a maximal limit.
candidate_data: Fish length-at-age and growth-parameter compilations (e.g. FishBase growth data) and reptile growth records in AnAge.

label: Adult size results from both the rate and the duration of growth
claim: The size an animal finally attains results from both its rate and its duration of growth: some species are larger because they grow faster (rabbit versus guinea-pig), others because they grow for longer (man versus rabbit).
quote: The size ultimately attained is a resultant of the rate, and of the duration, of growth. It is in the main true, as Minot has said, that the rabbit is bigger than the guinea-pig because he grows the faster; but that man is bigger than the rabbit because he goes on growing for a longer time.
measurable_quantities: age at cessation of growth or maturity
candidate_data: Species-level life-history and growth databases (AnAge, PanTHERIA, AnimalTraits).

label: Human length growth peaks in velocity around the fifth month before birth
claim: The human curve of growth in length has a point of inflection about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: before it growth velocity continually increases, and after it, though growth remains rapid, velocity falls away.
quote: It will at once be seen that there is a “point of inflection” somewhere about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: up to that date growth proceeds with a continually increasing velocity; but after that date, though growth is still rapid, its velocity tends to fall away.
candidate_data: Foetal growth standards from ultrasound studies (e.g. INTERGROWTH-21st foetal growth data, WHO foetal growth charts).

label: Growth rate is interrupted at physiological epochs such as birth, puberty, metamorphosis
claim: Curves of growth show well-marked interruptions or changes of rate at physiological epochs such as birth and puberty, in man and in other animals, and most strikingly in animals that undergo a regular metamorphosis.
quote: Just as the human curve of growth has its slight but well-marked interruptions, or variations in rate, coinciding with such epochs as birth and puberty, so is it with other animals, and this phenomenon is particularly striking in the case of animals which undergo a regular metamorphosis.
scope: animals, including man, mouse, silkworm, tadpole
measurable_quantities: growth velocity around birth, weaning, puberty, moults and metamorphosis
candidate_data: Longitudinal growth records of laboratory animals and insects (e.g. published mouse growth curves from the Mouse Phenome Database, insect larval growth datasets on Dryad).

label: Metamorphosis is often, perhaps always, accompanied by loss of bulk and weight
claim: Negative growth, an actual loss of bulk and weight, often and perhaps always accompanies metamorphosis, as in the eel, the silkworm before pupation and the frog tadpole.
quote: The negative growth, or actual loss of bulk and weight which often, and perhaps always, accompanies metamorphosis, is well shewn in the case of the eel.
measurable_quantities: body mass and dimensions before and after metamorphosis
candidate_data: Published larval-to-juvenile body-size datasets for amphibians, insects and anguillid eels (e.g. Dryad metamorphosis size datasets).

label: Variability of stature and weight tracks the rate of growth
claim: The coefficient of variability of human stature and weight falls when the rate of growth diminishes and rises again during the adolescent acceleration, so that variability is a function of the rate of growth.
quote: We see, in short, that the amount of _variability_ in stature or in weight is a function of the _rate of growth_ in these magnitudes, though we are not yet in a position to equate the terms precisely, one with another.
measurable_quantities: coefficient of variation of stature and weight by age
candidate_data: Growth reference datasets reporting age-specific standard deviations (WHO, CDC, national growth surveys).

section: Form as a function of growth rates
label: Each part has its own specific growth rate, on which specific morphology depends
claim: A large part of an organism's specific morphology depends on there being, besides an aggregate rate of growth of the whole, a characteristic specific rate of growth for each part or organ, so that small changes in these local rates soon produce striking differences of form.
quote: a very large part of the specific morphology of the organism depends upon the fact that there is not only an average, or aggregate, rate of growth common to the whole, but also a variation of rate in different parts of the organism, tending towards a specific rate characteristic of each different part or organ.
measurable_quantities: body proportions across species and ontogeny
candidate_data: Ontogenetic organ and limb growth datasets and comparative morphometrics (e.g. MorphoSource, Phenoscape, published relative-growth data on Dryad).

label: Organ size bears no constant ratio to body size through life, especially the brain
claim: There is no simple and constant relation, holding throughout life, between the size of the whole body and that of organs such as brain, heart and liver; the brain in particular falls from about one-eighth of body weight at birth to about one-fiftieth at twenty-five.
quote: It is plain, then, that there is no simple and direct relation, holding good _throughout life_, between the size of the body as a whole and that of the organs we have just discussed; and the changing ratio of magnitude is especially marked in the case of the brain
candidate_data: Autopsy organ-weight reference datasets by age and comparative ontogenetic organ-mass data.

label: Plaice weight-length coefficient peaks near the size of sexual maturity
claim: In plaice the weight-length coefficient k = W/L^3 is not constant but rises to a maximum and then slowly declines with increasing size, the maximum falling near 30 cm, about the size at which sexual maturity begins.
quote: we see that _k_ is by no means constant, but steadily increases to a maximum, and afterwards slowly declines with the increasing size of the fish
candidate_data: Fisheries survey length-weight records and maturity data (e.g. ICES DATRAS survey data, FishBase length-weight relationships).

label: Seasonal cycle in fish weight at fixed length is caused by spawning
claim: In plaice of fixed length, weight falls from about November to March or April and is restored between May or June and November, a periodic change caused wholly by spawning and the subsequent rebuilding of tissues and gonads, so that the spawning season can be determined from length and weight alone.
quote: With unchanging length, the weight and therefore the bulk of the fish falls off from about November to March or April, and again between May or June and November the bulk and weight are gradually restored. The explanation is simple, and depends wholly on the process of spawning, and on the subsequent building up again of the tissues and the reproductive organs.
scope: plaice and similar seasonally spawning fishes
measurable_quantities: weight at fixed length by month
candidate_data: Monthly fisheries sampling of length, weight and maturity stage (e.g. ICES survey and market-sampling data).

label: Growth has a van’t Hoff temperature coefficient like a chemical reaction
claim: Van’t Hoff’s law, that reaction velocity is multiplied by a constant factor for each degree of temperature rise, applies with qualifications to growth, so that growth has a temperature coefficient (about 2 to 3 per 10 °C, of the same order as chemical reactions).
quote: Van’t Hoff’s law, which has become a fundamental principle of chemical mechanics, is likewise applicable (with certain qualifications) to the phenomena of vital chemistry; and it follows that, on very much the same lines, we may speak of the “temperature coefficient” of growth.
scope: growth and development of plants and animals within normal temperature limits
measurable_quantities: growth or development rate at different temperatures
candidate_data: Compilations of thermal performance and development-rate data for ectotherms and plants (e.g. published Q10 and thermal performance curve datasets on Dryad).

label: Optimum temperature curves arise from acceleration combined with cumulative damage
claim: Growth rate has an optimum temperature because temperature both accelerates growth according to van’t Hoff’s law and progressively damages or fatigues the organism, so the optimum curve is a complex resultant rather than a primary phenomenon.
quote: It would seem to be this double effect of temperature in the case of the organism which gives us our “optimum” curves, which are the expression, accordingly, not of a primary phenomenon, but of a more or less complex resultant.
scope: physiological processes, especially growth, in plants and animals
measurable_quantities: growth rate versus exposure duration at high temperature
candidate_data: Thermal performance curve datasets with time-dependent exposure for plants and ectotherms (e.g. published thermal tolerance datasets on Dryad).

label: Common temperate plants share a growth optimum near 26 °C
claim: The optimum temperature for growth is much the same, about 26 °C, for the common plants of temperate climates, and considerably higher for plants of warmer regions such as melon and maize.
quote: this optimum temperature is very much the same for all the common plants of our own climate which have as yet been studied; in them it is somewhere about 26° C. (or say 77° F.), or about the temperature of a warm summer’s day
scope: temperate and warm-climate plants (root and shoot elongation)
candidate_data: Plant thermal response compilations and TRY plant traits database entries on temperature optima.

label: Seasonal growth in fish and man follows a damped sine curve
claim: In fishes such as plaice and haddock, and in man, growth is slower in winter than in summer, as if an annual sine curve were superimposed on the growth curve, and the amplitude of this fluctuation dies away as growth slows, giving a damped sine curve.
quote: in short, our phenomenon is simply expressed by what is known as a “damped sine-curve.” Exactly the same thing occurs in man, though neither in his case nor in that of the fish have we sufficient data for its complete illustration.
candidate_data: Fish otolith and scale increment datasets and human seasonal growth studies with sub-annual measurement.

label: Arizona tree rings show a regular 150-year climate periodicity
claim: Century-smoothed annual ring widths of Arizona yellow pines show that the climate of Arizona over the past 500 years fluctuated with a regular period of almost exactly 150 years, probably mainly in moisture rather than temperature.
quote: from which we seem compelled to draw the direct conclusion that the climate of Arizona, during the last 500 years, has fluctuated with a regular periodicity of almost precisely 150 years.
scope: Arizona climate, 1390s–1910s, inferred from ponderosa (yellow) pine rings
candidate_data: International Tree-Ring Data Bank (ITRDB) ponderosa pine chronologies from Arizona and Southwest drought reconstructions (e.g. North American Drought Atlas).

label: Growth rate depends largely on water uptake (turgor) as well as metabolism
claim: A large part of growth, in animals and more conspicuously in plants, depends on turgor and osmotic conditions: the velocity of growth depends largely on the amount of water taken into the cells as well as on chemical metabolism.
quote: A large part of the phenomenon of growth, both in animals and still more conspicuously in plants, is associated with “turgor,” that is to say, is dependent on osmotic conditions; in other words, the velocity of growth depends in great measure (as we have already seen, p. 113) on the amount of water taken up into the living cells
scope: growing cells of plants and animals, especially plant elongation and early embryos
candidate_data: Plant cell expansion and turgor measurement studies and embryo water-content time series (published datasets on Dryad).

label: Brine-shrimp abdomen grows relatively longer the saltier the water
claim: In brine-shrimps (Artemia), increasing salinity changes the relative rates of growth of body parts, the abdomen growing relatively longer compared with the cephalothorax the salter the water, so that forms described as distinct species correspond to ranges of water density.
quote: _Pari passu_ with these changes, there is a marked change in the relative lengths of the fore and hind portions of the body, that is to say, of the “cephalothorax” and abdomen: the latter growing relatively longer, the salter the water.
scope: brine-shrimps (Artemia) in waters of varying salinity
candidate_data: Artemia morphometric studies across salinity gradients and rearing experiments (published datasets on Dryad).

label: The organic curve of growth resembles the velocity curve of chemical autocatalysis
claim: The normal curve of growth of an organism closely resembles the velocity curve of an autocatalytic chemical reaction, with a phase of increasing acceleration, a phase in which limiting conditions reduce acceleration, and usually a final phase of retardation and loss of mass; but only a resemblance, not an identity, can yet be asserted.
quote: it is sufficiently clear that the normal “curve of growth” of an organism, in all its general features, very closely resembles the velocity-curve of chemical autocatalysis.
candidate_data: Growth-curve datasets fitted with logistic and related models (e.g. published animal and plant growth curves on Dryad, AnAge).

label: Internal secretions and other substances accelerate growth and alter proportions
claim: Substances inside and outside the organism, such as thyroid and pituitary secretions or iodine compounds, can accelerate growth in a way that changes not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.
quote: We may take it, then, as an established fact, whose full extent and bearings are still awaiting investigation, that there exist substances both within and without the organism which have a marvellous power of accelerating growth, and of doing so in such a way as to affect not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.
scope: animals (tadpoles, mammals, birds), with parallels in plants
measurable_quantities: growth rates of specific organs under hormone treatment
candidate_data: Experimental endocrinology datasets on thyroid hormone in amphibian metamorphosis and growth hormone effects on body proportions (published studies on Dryad).

label: Natural selection removes forms rather than originating them
claim: Since forms, including exaggerated ones such as the great Secondary reptiles and Tertiary mammals, can arise from changes in growth, natural selection is needed to explain their disappearance rather than their appearance; in general its function is not to originate but to remove.
quote: And we then, I think, draw near to the conclusion that what is true of these is universally true, and that the great function of natural selection is not to originate, but to remove
candidate_data: none known

label: Velocity of regenerative growth varies inversely as about the square of time
claim: After its early maximum, the velocity of regenerative growth (tadpole tails) falls off inversely as some power of the time since injury, approximately as 1/T^2, so that V T^2 is nearly constant.
quote: And in this particular case, the equation _V_ _T_^2 = constant, holds very nearly true; that is to say the velocity varies, or tends to vary, inversely as the square of the time.
scope: regenerating tadpole tails, possibly regeneration generally
measurable_quantities: regenerated length versus days after amputation
candidate_data: Time-course regeneration measurements in amphibian larvae and zebrafish fins (published datasets on Dryad).

label: Regeneration is ordinary growth, with the same curve as growth from zero
claim: Regeneration is a particular case of growth obeying the same laws; the regeneration curve (short latent period, rapid rise to a maximum velocity, then slow decline) only appears different because ordinary growth curves start at birth, and a complete growth curve from zero has the same essential features.
quote: A complete curve of growth, starting from zero, has the same essential characteristics as the regeneration curve.
measurable_quantities: embryonic growth velocity versus time from conception
candidate_data: Regeneration time-course data (amphibians, zebrafish) alongside prenatal growth curves (published datasets on Dryad).

label: Claw reversal after amputation depends on regeneration versus growth rates
claim: Whether an amputated large crustacean claw regenerates as the large claw, or the claws exchange roles, depends on the ratio between the regenerative growth rate of the amputated claw and the growth rate of the uninjured claw, since claw form follows claw size.
quote: It depends upon the respective rates of growth, upon a ratio between the rate of regeneration and the rate of growth of the uninjured limb
scope: Crustacea with asymmetric claws (lobster, Alpheus, crabs)
measurable_quantities: claw size and form over successive moults
candidate_data: Snapping shrimp and crab claw-regeneration experiment data (published studies on Dryad).

label: Reproduction by fission is a physical tendency to segment plus regeneration
claim: Reproduction by fission in worm-like animals consists essentially of the physical tendency of a long semi-fluid tube to break into segments, combined with ordinary regeneration, which explains its occurrence in zoologically unrelated animals and its absence in some close relatives.
quote: If we add to this natural tendency towards fission of a cylindrical or tubular worm, the ordinary phenomenon of regeneration, we have all that is essentially implied in “reproduction by fission.”
scope: worms and worm-like animals that reproduce by fission
candidate_data: Phylogenetic trait data on asexual fission in annelids and flatworms combined with body-size data (e.g. published comparative datasets).

label: Growth velocity peaks and falls because surface resistance suddenly increases
claim: The abrupt change from increasing to decreasing growth velocity is more likely due to a sudden increase of resistance, such as the formation of a comparatively firm skin during histological differentiation, than to a decline of internal growth forces; the later slowing reflects waning growth forces against rising superficial resistance.
quote: I take it that the sudden arrest of velocity is much more likely to be due to a sudden increase of resistance than to a sudden diminution of internal energies: in other words, I suspect that it is coincident with some notable event of histological differentiation, such as the rapid formation of a comparatively firm skin
scope: growing organisms generally, including regenerating tissues
measurable_quantities: timing of skin or tissue differentiation
candidate_data: Developmental tissue-mechanics measurements paired with growth time series (published embryo mechanics datasets).

label: Form changes follow the same route in individual development and racial history
claim: Changes of form produced by varying rates of growth are the same phenomenon in individual development and in the differences between species; a transformation from one form to another follows the same course whether it happens within a lifetime or over ancestral history, which accounts for much of von Baer's law of recapitulation.
quote: From one form, or ratio of magnitude, to another there is but one straight and direct road of transformation, be the journey taken fast or slow; and if the transformation take place at all, it will in all likelihood proceed in the self-same way, whether it occur within the life-time of an individual or during the long ancestral history of a race.
scope: ontogeny and phylogeny of organic form
candidate_data: Geometric morphometric datasets with ontogenetic and phylogenetic series (e.g. MorphoSource, Paleobiology Database occurrence and size data).
